extracted.intended_audience: beginner stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and open-mic performers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for constructing and testing Rule-of-3 jokes for stand-up and related comedic writing, with examples, anti-patterns, and stage-testing advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 3 structure
rubrics_metrics.description: List three things — the first two set up an expectation and the third breaks it in a surprising or absurd way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychologically, comedy thrives on pattern + surprise. Two feels incomplete and four feels like a list; three creates a pattern after item two that you can then subvert with item three. Example: 'My mom taught me three life lessons — to always tell the truth, to respect my elders, and to lie convincingly when relatives ask my salary.' The laugh lives in the contrast between items 1–2 and item 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup (Element 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the topic and tone in the first item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item one sets context — keep it clear and concise so the audience knows what you're talking about and the tone you're aiming for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement (Element 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm the pattern with the second item so the audience predicts the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item two should reinforce the expectation created by item one (similar length and tone), building trust and making the audience mentally finish the pattern before you deliver the twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline (Element 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twist, escalate, or completely betray the pattern on the third item; this is where the laugh sits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third item should break the audience's prediction — it may escalate, invert, or be absurdly specific. It often needs slightly more space (usually a bit longer) to land. Examples in the article show moral contrast, escalation to absurdity, or hyper-specific details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and hyper-detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the third item specific and concrete to increase comedic payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyper-specific third items (e.g., a bored DJ playing a 2014 remix, a cousin in Canada sending a single 'Ok' once every leap year) create recognition and surprise, which amplifies laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use increasing scale or absurdity across the three items so the third is a heightened consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items one and two should be plausible; item three escalates the scenario into something more extreme or absurd (e.g., 'small ceremony', 'just close family', '1,200 guests and one bored DJ'). Escalation sharpens the punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a rhythmic pattern: short, short, then slightly longer for the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three has a natural musicality. Items one and two should be roughly equal in length; item three usually carries the twist and can be a touch longer. Breathe between beats and use timing to let the audience build expectation before the reveal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep items one and two concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overcomplicating the setup; long, winding setups kill rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items one and two are the runway, not the plane. Keep them crisp so the audience can spot the pattern quickly — verbosity here slows recognition and weakens the pay-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a predictable third punch
rubrics_metrics.description: The third item must be surprising; if the audience can guess it, the joke fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is non-negotiable. If your twist is foreseeable, rework it so the third travels further from the expected pattern. Test with strangers — if they predict it, change it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing: don't rush the beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the audience time to detect the pattern; rushing robs the joke of setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you speed through items one and two, the audience won't have time to form the expectation that makes the third funny. If the audience laughs on item two, that's a sign your third punch is weaker than your setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain strong contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: The third item should differ in tone or content from the first two to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the third feels similar in tone to the first two, there is no twist. The further the third travels from the expected pattern (in moral stance, specificity, absurdity, etc.), the harder the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't force the Rule of 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Rule of 3 only when it fits; don't shoehorn it into every joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the third element feels stretched or contrived, drop it and consider a one-liner or different structure. Overuse makes the device predictable — a 6-minute set should use it sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit frequency per set
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Rule of 3 two or three times maximum in a 6-minute set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated use within a short set makes the structure predictable; spacing and variety retain surprise and freshness for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice with daily life and write often
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate material by writing multiple Rule-of-3 jokes every day on ordinary topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick topics (boss, traffic, landlords) and force yourself to produce three-joke variants — practice sharpens instinct for what makes a surprising third item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test jokes on real humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Try jokes on friends and at open mics to see if the third item produces laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real metric is audience reaction. If item three gets the laugh, structure works. If not, rewrite. Use beginner-friendly open mics (no audition) to iterate quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record open mics and analyze
rubrics_metrics.description: Record performances and listen back to evaluate where laughs occur and whether timing is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for whether the room laughs on item three (good) or item two (problem). Use recordings to spot pacing, trim fluff, and refine rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play with rhythm deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust lengths and phrasing of items one–three to optimize musicality and surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make items one and two roughly equal and punch item three with slightly more space. Experiment with pauses and cadence to maximize tension and release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit ruthlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut every word that doesn't earn its place; the Rule of 3 is a tight format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluff kills rhythm and reduces the effectiveness of the third item. Remove unnecessary words so the setup/signal is sharp and the punch lands cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications/formats for Rule of 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Rule of 3 across different comedy forms: lists, storytelling, observational bits, and character-based humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists: three direct items. Storytelling: three escalating beats inside a narrative. Observational: group three small truths. Character-based: give a character three traits where the third undermines the first two. Choose the format that fits the premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third item need not be funny alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The third item may only be funny in contrast to the first two; standalone funniness is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the humor is created by the relationship between items — the third's absurdity compared to mundane first two is what elicits laughter. Don't overrequire the third to be independently hilarious.
